verse-prepare — the local compression step#

A DCC export is sized for the DCC, not for delivery: a 4K texture on a door handle, the same chair exported forty times, buffers nothing references. On archviz exports that is where the 2–40 GB comes from, and it is why uploads used to stop at 512 MB.

verse-prepare rewrites a GLB so that **what travels is what a visitor can ever see** — without changing what they see. It runs in three places:

WhereHowTextures
Blender / Unreal / Unity plug-insautomatically, between export and uploadbase colour → JPEG 92 (opaque only), everything else lossless
the ingest serveron every upload that arrives without the markerlossless
your shell / CIverse-prepare in.glb -o out.glbyour flags

Files that went through it carry asset.extras.verse.prepared and may be up to 20 GB on the resumable upload (POST /v1/ingest/begin with "prepared": true; the server verifies the marker at commit). Plain files are accepted up to the plan's raw upload limit (rawUploadMB) and the server prepares them itself.

What it does#

  1. Texel-density right-sizing. For every image, the world-space size of the surfaces that sample it is measured from the triangles themselves (world area ÷ UV area, per primitive, through node transforms and KHR_texture_transform scale). The image keeps the resolution a visitor standing at arm's length can resolve — --texels-per-metre, default 2048 px/m (one texel per screen pixel at ~0.5 m on a 1080p screen) — and nothing more. Never upscaled, never below --min-dim (256), never above --max-dim (4096). The largest use of an image decides, so a texture shared by a wall and a tile keeps the wall's detail.
  2. Re-encode. Opaque base colour goes to JPEG (quality 92, invisible at the right-sized resolution). Lightmaps, emissive, normals, roughness, occlusion and anything with alpha stay PNG — banding and normal artefacts never appear. --lossless keeps everything PNG. Images that need neither a resize nor a format change pass through byte for byte.
  3. Dedupe. Identical images, identical accessors and identical meshes (same primitives, same materials) collapse to one copy; nodes re-point to the survivor — glTF instancing. --no-dedupe switches it off.
  4. Strip. Buffer views and accessors nothing references any more are dropped and the binary chunk is rebuilt tight.

Positions pass through bit-identical by default: the compiler's cluster DAG is the right place to handle triangle density, and unchanged positions keep the fidelity harness meaningful (and the compiler's geometry cache warm — see --weld / --simplify-error below for the two opt-in passes that do move vertices). Unused vertex attributes are dropped (lossless), and --max-tris-per-m2 can thin over-dense meshes on request. Quantized output (KHR_mesh_quantization) is deliberately not produced: the ingest server would have to expand it in memory before the compiler reads it, which is the wrong trade for 2 GB files.

On the flagship flat (3.1 M triangles, 399 textures) the Draco-decoded export goes 283 → 190 MB in 0.9 s: 19 textures right-sized (plants, vases and books sampled above 4000 px/m), 4 meshes instanced, 1 183 stale buffer views dropped. On exports with 4K textures everywhere the ratio is far larger — the tool prints what it did to every image.

CLI#

Code
verse-prepare in.glb [-o out.glb] [--texels-per-metre 2048] [--max-dim 4096]
             [--min-dim 256] [--lossless] [--jpeg-quality 92] [--no-dedupe]
             [--keep-attributes] [--max-tris-per-m2 N]
             [--weld [E]] [--simplify-error E]
             [--json report.json|-] [--dry-run] [--quiet]
  • Output defaults to in.prepared.glb.
  • --keep-attributes keeps vertex attributes the pass would otherwise drop (a TANGENT with no normal map, an all-white COLOR_n, a TEXCOORD_k no texture samples). Stripping is lossless; it is on by default.
  • --max-tris-per-m2 N (off by default, lossy): primitives denser than N triangles per square metre of world surface are simplified to that density with meshopt. Positions are never moved and vertex arrays are untouched, so the upload shrinks only by the index list; the real win is a lighter compile and stream. 2000 removed 1.97 M of the flat's 3.1 M triangles. Leave it off for product close-ups.
  • --weld [E] (off by default; moves vertices, lossless to the tolerance): merges vertices whose positions lie within E metres of each other (world space, through the mesh's largest instance scale; --weld alone = 0.1 mm) and whose other attributes — normal, UV, tangent, colour — are bit-identical, so UV-chart seams and hard edges survive. The first vertex is canonical and keeps its position; the others snap to it, the vertex buffers are rewritten to the survivors, indices are remapped and triangles that collapsed are dropped. Points/lines, morph-target and skinned primitives are left alone. Exports that duplicate every vertex per triangle (some CAD/BIM paths) shrink by 3–6× in geometry; the compiler's own position-weld then finds nothing left to do.
  • --simplify-error E (off by default; lossy within E): meshopt attribute-aware simplification with an absolute positional error bound of E metres (world space) — 0.001 means no surface moves more than a millimetre. Normals and UVs steer the collapse (a ~15° normal change or a quarter-UV shift costs as much as the full bound), borders are locked so neighbouring primitives never crack, and the vertex buffers are rewritten to the surviving vertices — unlike --max-tris-per-m2, the saving is real bytes, not an index list. Runs after --weld and after the density pass when both are given. The report carries verticesWelded / verticesSimplified; the prepared marker records both tolerances.
  • --dry-run measures and reports without writing — the estimate step.
  • --decode-meshopt only decodes EXT_meshopt_compression / KHR_meshopt_compression to plain buffer views and writes the GLB (the ingest server's normalizer). A meshopt input to the full pass is decoded the same way first (3.0.0-beta.1).
  • --json - prints the report to stdout: per-image before/after dimensions and bytes, the source texel density, the action taken (kept, resized, re-encoded, dropped, duplicate of N), dedupe counts, triangles, seconds.
  • stderr carries progress: prepare images i/n lines (what the plug-ins show) and one line per image that changed.
  • Exit 0 on success, 2 on usage, 1 when the input is refused. Refused inputs say why: Draco compression (export with compression off — the server still accepts Draco for direct uploads), external buffers (.gltf + .bin; export a single .glb).

The input is memory-mapped: a 20 GB export is measured in place, and only the images and the surviving buffer views are copied.

Building and bundling the binary#

From the repo root, cargo build --release -p verse-compile produces target/release/verse-prepare next to verse-compile (the Dockerfile copies it into the image; the ingest server spawns it). The Tools GitHub Actions workflow (.github/workflows/tools.yml, run it from the Actions tab or push a tools-v* tag) builds four binaries:

ArtifactFor
verse-prepare-darwin-arm64Apple Silicon Macs
verse-prepare-darwin-x64Intel Macs
verse-prepare-windows-x64.exeWindows
verse-prepare-linux-x64Linux

Drop them into integrations/bin/ (gitignored) and build the plug-ins:

  • Blender — python3 integrations/blender/make_extension.py puts them under verse_publish/bin/ inside the zip with the exec bit kept.
  • Unity — sh integrations/unity/make_tarball.sh copies them to the package's Tools~/.
  • Unreal — sh integrations/unreal/VersePublish/make_plugin_zip.sh copies them to the plug-in's Resources/bin/.

All three plug-ins upload large files through the resumable begin/part/commit flow, so prepared files up to 20 GB work from every editor.

Each plug-in looks for the tool in this order: the path set in its preferences, the bundled copy, then PATH (the Unreal plug-in also finds the repo's target/release/verse-prepare when it is built inside the repo, and integrations/unreal/VersePublish/bundle_prepare.sh builds the Mac binaries into its Resources/bin/ for a from-source build).

Non-finite numbers. JSON has no inf / NaN, but some exporters print them anyway (Unreal 5.8 wrote "ior":inf). verse-prepare, the compiler and the Unreal plug-in replace each with a safe value for its field — ior → 1.5, factors and colours clamped to 0..1 (NaN → the spec default), attenuationDistance / light range / camera zfar removed (absent means infinite), transforms → identity — log every fix and list it in the report's warnings.

In the plug-ins#

The publish flow becomes export → prepare → upload → compile. The prepare phase shows the tool's own progress (Preparing textures 120/400), then the result (Prepared 2 480 → 310 MB (212 textures right-sized)). Preferences: Prepare before upload (on), the binary path, Texels per metre (2048), Lossless textures (off).

Without the tool, exports upload as they are (resumably, up to the plan's raw upload limit) and the server prepares them; the plug-in logs the install hint.

Choosing texels per metre#

SettingMeansUse
10241:1 texels at ~1 m on 1080plarge exteriors, previews, bandwidth-first
20481:1 at ~0.5 minteriors, furniture, the default
40961:1 at ~0.25 mproduct close-ups, hero materials you walk right up to

The compiler keeps its own ceilings after this step (2048² streamed tiers, 4096² hero tier), so a higher setting only matters for sources that are actually that dense.
